title: Book value, earnings, cash, and ratios
hook: A company can change the world and still be a bad investment. The financial statements are how you tell the difference.
objectives: Separate book value from market value, and read the market-to-book ratio.
Walk the income statement to net income, and read EPS and P/E correctly.
Sort cash flow items into operating, investing and financing, and match each ratio family to the question it answers.

steps.title: A great business is not a great investment

blocks.md:
The professor used Anthropic's leaked IPO prospectus as a cautionary case. The company reported rapid revenue growth, but its costs grew too, and the profit claim left out the biggest cost, model training.

> "You can have a fantastic business and a fantastic technology... That does not mean it's a fantastic business."

The gap between a great company and a great investment is the price you pay.

blocks.title: If 1,000% growth kept going
blocks.caption: Start of $4.59B is the 2025 revenue reported in the leaked filing. For scale, world output is on the order of $100 trillion (about 100,000 on this scale; a rough figure, not from the lecture). The professor said 'about six years' to pass Earth's revenue; at these numbers it is closer to five. His point stands: 1,000% a year cannot continue.

blocks.headline: Inside Anthropic's IPO Filing: What's Really Behind Its $42B Loss
blocks.tieIn: The article reports 2025 revenue of $4.59B, an operating loss of $8.06B and a net loss of about $41.6B. It attributes roughly $34B of that net loss to an accounting charge tied mostly to earlier financing that could turn into shares. Operating loss and net loss are different lines of the income statement, which is why you read each one before judging a valuation.

blocks.q: Why must future cash flows be 'massive' to justify a high valuation today?
options: They arrive far in the future and get discounted, and today's losses dig a hole to fill
They arrive today, so any positive number justifies the valuation
Discounting makes distant cash flows larger, so little is needed
Valuation depends only on the share price, not on cash flows
blocks.why: The professor's point: distant cash is discounted to a smaller number, and large negative cash flows now must be offset by even larger positives later.

blocks.md:
**Market value** is what the market says the company is worth: share price times shares outstanding. A billion shares at $120 is a $120 billion company.

**Book value** is rooted in the balance sheet: assets minus liabilities. Market value can swing with investor psychology while the balance sheet barely moves. It can also be higher for good reasons, such as a brand or intellectual property that nobody can copy (a moat).

blocks.title: Two ways to say what a company is worth

rows.label: Formula
cells: Price per share x shares outstanding

blocks.title: Market-to-book ratio
blocks.caption: Value stocks sit near 1.5x to 2x. Buffett looks harder when the ratio reaches 3x or 4x. Growth stocks have no ceiling.

blocks.q: A firm has 2 billion shares at $45 and book equity of $60 billion. What is its market-to-book ratio?

steps.title: The income statement, line by line

blocks.md:
The income statement shows revenues and expenses over a period. It starts at total sales and subtracts costs until it reaches net income.

Operating income is the business before interest and taxes, and this is where the professor objected to Anthropic's 'profitable' claim: it left out training costs, which he called "earnings before the bad stuff." Depreciation lowers income and taxes but is not a cash cost.

blocks.title: From $1,000M of sales to net income ($M, illustrative)

frames.title: Gross profit
frames.text: Subtract the cost of making the product.

frames.title: Operating income
frames.text: Subtract selling and admin (SG&A) 120, R&D 80, and depreciation and amortization 50. This is the business itself.

frames.title: Pre-tax income
frames.text: Interest on loans is a separate skill from running the business. Subtract it now.

frames.title: Net income
frames.text: Taxes at 25% leave the bottom line.

blocks.q: Why is excluding model training from operating costs a red flag for an AI lab?
options: Training is a one-time investment that is already finished
Taxes are charged only on training costs
Training never stops under competition, so it is a core running cost
Training costs are not real expenses
blocks.why: The professor's argument: if training is permanent, it belongs in operating costs. If it were a one-time investment, leaving it out would be more defensible.

blocks.md:
**EPS** = net income / shares: how much of the earnings are yours per share. **P/E** = price / EPS: what you pay for $1 of earnings.

> "Expensive is relative to how much price you're paying for earnings."

Berkshire trades near $751,000 a share yet has a P/E around 12, among the cheapest in the world. SpaceX had no earnings, so no P/E at all.

blocks.title: Rounded P/E ratios the professor quoted
blocks.caption: Investors pay more now for earnings they expect later. SpaceX has no earnings, so it has no bar.

blocks.q: A company doubles its share count with the same earnings, and the share price stays put. What happens to EPS and P/E?
blocks.why: Same earnings spread over twice the shares halves EPS. With the price unchanged, price / EPS doubles. This is dilution.

blocks.md:
The cash flow statement starts from net income, then adjusts to real cash. Depreciation is added back, since no cash left. Customers who owe you (receivables) mean income without cash, so an increase is deducted.

> "I want my accounts receivable to be paid off real quick and my accounts payable to be paid off in the future."

The three sections are operating, investing and financing.

blocks.prompt: Which section does each item belong to?
blocks.why: Dividends and loans are financing (the lecture slip put dividends under investing, but the slides list them under financing). CapEx and asset sales are investing. Depreciation and working-capital changes adjust operating cash.

blocks.title: From net income to change in cash ($ thousands, illustrative)

frames.title: Start with net income
frames.text: Net income is the first row.

frames.title: Operating adjustments
frames.text: Add back depreciation 100. Receivables rose 150 (cash not yet collected). Payables rose 80 (cash not yet paid). Inventory rose 60 (cash spent on stock).

frames.title: Net change in cash
frames.text: This matches the change in cash on the balance sheet, so the statements tie together.

blocks.q: Accounts receivable rose by $150k this year. What does that do to operating cash flow relative to net income?
options: Raises it, but only after a year
blocks.why: Sales were booked in income but the cash has not arrived, so the increase is deducted. Cash was not collected.

blocks.md:
There are dozens of ratios, and you will not memorize them all. Each gives one lens on the business, and none is enough alone. Ratios also let you compare firms of different sizes, such as Ferrari and Tesla on operating margin.

Watch how they change over time. A cash ratio that halves in a year is a red flag worth chasing.

rows.label: Profitability
cells: How much profit per $1 of sales?

rows.label: Liquidity
cells: Can we pay our near-term debts?
Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities

rows.label: Working capital
cells: How fast does product turn into cash?
Inventory days = inventory / daily sales (500 cups at 100 a day = 5 days)

rows.label: Leverage
cells: How much do we lean on debt?

blocks.title: Current ratio
blocks.caption: Below 1.0x, short-term bills exceed short-term assets.

blocks.title: DuPont: ROE as three business levers

frames.title: Profit margin
frames.text: How much of each sales dollar becomes profit.

frames.title: Asset turnover
frames.text: How hard the assets work to produce sales.

frames.title: Equity multiplier
frames.text: How much of the assets are financed by more than equity.

frames.title: Multiply
frames.text: Sales and assets cancel, leaving net income over book equity.

blocks.q: A target has low ROE. Its margin is healthy and its leverage is normal, but asset turnover is weak. Where does an operator focus?
options: Getting more sales out of the same assets
blocks.why: DuPont splits ROE so you can see which lever is failing. Here it is asset turnover.

recap: A great business is not automatically a great investment. The price you pay relative to what you get is what matters.
Book value = assets - liabilities (can be negative). Market value = price x shares (cannot be). Market-to-book flags disconnects.
Income statement runs sales to net income. EPS = NI / shares. P/E = price / EPS. Price per share alone says nothing about expensive.
Cash flow starts at net income and adjusts to cash across operating, investing and financing. Each ratio family is one lens.

quiz.q: A company has 500 million shares at $80. What is its market value?
Which statement about a great technology company is the professor's point?
options: Share price is irrelevant for any investment
A high price can make even a great business a poor investment
Only unprofitable firms can be good investments
quiz.why: Microsoft in the '90s, internet stocks, and Anthropic all illustrate that business quality and investment quality differ by the price paid.

quiz.q: Net income is $60M, there are 20M shares, and the price is $90. What is the P/E?
Why is depreciation added back on the cash flow statement?
options: It is a real cash payment
It reduced net income but no cash left the firm
quiz.why: Depreciation lowers accounting income but uses no cash, so you put it back to find cash generated.

quiz.q: Margin is 5%, asset turnover is 2, and the equity multiplier is 3. What is ROE?

flashcards.back: Book = assets - liabilities (equity), can be negative. Market = price x shares outstanding, cannot be negative.
Market value / book value. Value stocks are low (about 1.5x to 2x). Growth stocks have no ceiling. Buffett looks harder at 3x to 4x.
EPS = net income / shares. P/E = price / EPS, the price paid per $1 of earnings. A high share price is not the same as expensive.
Operating: business activity and working capital. Investing: capex and asset sales. Financing: loans and dividends.
Collect receivables quickly and push payables out. Dell got paid before building the computer.
ROE = (NI / Sales) x (Sales / Assets) x (Assets / Equity): margin x asset turnover x equity multiplier.
